explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Luke says Jesus was "…led by the Spirit into the wilderness…" (Luke 4:1). He didn't wander out there by accident or because He lost the map. The same verse says He was full of the Holy Spirit when it happened.

Good guess, but the leader here is named. Luke says Jesus was "…led by the Spirit into the wilderness…" (Luke 4:1). Not one disciple gets a mention in these thirteen verses. So the Spirit does the leading, and Jesus does the following.

Angels do come up in this passage, but not as the guides. Luke says Jesus was "…led by the Spirit into the wilderness…" (Luke 4:1). Angels are mentioned only in the devil's own quote (Luke 4:10-11). Here the Spirit is the one doing the leading.
Right, friend. Luke says Jesus "…ate nothing during those days, and when they had ended, He was hungry." (Luke 4:2). Plain as day. Forty days with no food, and I'd be hungry by the second one.

Not this time, baker. Luke says Jesus "…ate nothing during those days, and when they had ended, He was hungry." (Luke 4:2). So the text says He was hungry, plain and simple. Forty days without food will do that to anybody, and I'm a stamper who gets cranky when the cooling rack runs empty.

Bread it is. The devil says, "If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread." (Luke 4:3). Jesus had eaten nothing for forty days, so bread was right where the dare landed. I'll be honest, a stone is a rough place to start baking.

Gold is a shiny guess, but that's not in this dare. The devil says, "If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread." (Luke 4:3). The dare was about food for a hungry Jesus. Gold would have been a different dare altogether.

Water, baker? I see where your head went, but nobody in this passage mentions it. The devil says, "If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread." (Luke 4:3). Stone to bread is the dare. I've stamped a lot of dough in my day, and a stone is the one thing I'd never ask to rise.

That's it, friend. Jesus answers, "It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone.’…" (Luke 4:4). He answers with the written Word. That's a good reminder for any of us who get hungry and want to give in.

explanations.answer: He turns the stone into bread
explanations.explanation: Plenty of us would have done it, baker. Me? I'd have been arguing with the stone. But what Luke records is Jesus answering, "It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone.’…" (Luke 4:4). That's the answer the passage gives.
He does speak, friend. Luke records that Jesus answered, "It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone.’…" (Luke 4:4). His answer is the written Word, and the devil isn't done asking yet.

Correct, baker. The devil says, "I will give You authority over all these kingdoms and all their glory…" (Luke 4:6). He's showing Jesus every kingdom of the world and offering the whole lot. That's a big offer, and I can't even offer you a whole batch without eating two.

Actually, the offer is real, friend. The devil says, "I will give You authority over all these kingdoms and all their glory…" (Luke 4:6). He had just shown Jesus all the kingdoms of the world in an instant (Luke 4:5). So authority over the kingdoms and their glory is what he puts on the table.
Yes, baker. The devil says, "So if You worship me, it will all be Yours." (Luke 4:7). There's the catch. Every offer has a price tag, and the price he names is worship.

Jerusalem is where round three happens, but it's not the price here. The devil says, "So if You worship me, it will all be Yours." (Luke 4:7). What he wants is worship. The offer has nothing to do with where Jesus stands.

Prayer isn't in this offer, friend. The devil says, "So if You worship me, it will all be Yours." (Luke 4:7). Picture a guy showing you the keys to a whole kingdom, and the fine print says WORSHIP ME. That's one expensive set of keys.
You got it, baker. Jesus answers, "It is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’…" (Luke 4:8). Worship and service both go to the Lord your God. That's His answer to the offer.

Not quite, friend. The devil's pitch was that Jesus worship him (Luke 4:7). But Jesus answers, "It is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’…" (Luke 4:8). The Scripture points to the Lord your God alone.

I get why you'd think that, baker, but angels aren't the answer. Jesus says, "It is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’…" (Luke 4:8). Worship and service go to the Lord your God, and Him only.

That's right, baker. The devil says, "For it is written: 'He will command His angels concerning You to guard You carefully…'" (Luke 4:10). Yes, he quotes the Bible. It's a good reminder that a verse can be quoted and still be pointed the wrong way.

No philosophers show up on that temple, friend. The devil says, "For it is written: 'He will command His angels concerning You to guard You carefully…'" (Luke 4:10). He backs up his dare with what is written. That's Scripture.

No legends in this one, baker. The devil says, "For it is written: 'He will command His angels concerning You to guard You carefully…'" (Luke 4:10). That phrase means Scripture. He picks up the same kind of words Jesus has been using.

explanations.answer: Put the Lord your God to the test
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus answers, "It also says, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’…" (Luke 4:12). Notice the word "also." Jesus isn't throwing out the devil's verse, He's setting another one beside it.

explanations.answer: Stand upon the pinnacle of the temple
explanations.explanation: Standing there is where Jesus already is, baker, so that's not the warning. He answers, "It also says, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’…" (Luke 4:12). The devil is the one who set Him on the pinnacle (Luke 4:9). The verse is about testing the Lord your God.

explanations.answer: Lean on the strength of your own hand
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a proverb, friend, but it isn't what Jesus says here. He answers, "It also says, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’…" (Luke 4:12). Nothing about hands or strength comes up in this passage. The warning is about testing the Lord your God.

I see why that sounds right, baker, but read the last verse again. Luke says, "When the devil had finished every temptation, he left Him until an opportune time." (Luke 4:13). He left Jesus for a while, with the words "…until an opportune time." hanging on the end. The text never says he was gone for good.

Right, baker. Luke says, "When the devil had finished every temptation, he left Him until an opportune time." (Luke 4:13). That "until" matters. He left for a while, and the text never says he's gone for good.
